mcqs.q: What is a *translation unit* in the C++ build model?
options: A single `.cpp` file after preprocessing (the source plus everything its `#include`s pulled in)
The final linked executable that the loader maps into memory
Any header file that has been guarded with `#pragma once`
The set of all `.o` files passed to the linker at once
mcqs.explanation: A translation unit is one `.cpp` file *after preprocessing*. The compiler sees exactly one TU at a time and knows nothing about the others, which is why it cannot inline a function defined in a different `.cpp` without LTO.

mcqs.q: A header contains `int counter = 0;` and is included by three `.cpp` files. What error results, and what is a correct fix?
options: An "undefined reference" link error; add `extern` in the header
A "multiple definition" link error; mark it `inline` (or move the definition to one `.cpp`)
No error at all; each TU gets its own private copy automatically
A preprocessor error; add an include guard
mcqs.explanation: A non-`inline` variable with external linkage defined in a header violates the One-Definition Rule across TUs, giving a multiple-definition link error. `inline int counter = 0;` (C++17 inline variables) or a single out-of-line definition fixes it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about `-Ofast` is TRUE?
options: It is identical to `-O2` but with faster compile times
It guarantees the same floating-point results as `-O0`
It implies `-ffast-math`, which breaks strict IEEE-754 semantics and is risky for pricing math
It optimizes purely for binary size like `-Os`
mcqs.explanation: `-Ofast` is `-O3` plus `-ffast-math`, which reorders/contracts floating-point operations and breaks IEEE-754 semantics. `-O2`/`-O3` keep IEEE semantics; `-ffast-math` does not, so `-Ofast` is rarely safe near pricing math.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between `std::vector<int> a(3);` and `std::vector<int> a{3};`?
options: Both create three elements equal to `0`
`a(3)` has one element `3`; `a{3}` has three elements all `0`
Both create one element equal to `3`
`a(3)` has three elements all `0`; `a{3}` has one element with value `3`
mcqs.explanation: `(3)` is direct-init that selects the `(size_t, value)` constructor giving three value-initialized `0`s; `{3}` prefers the `initializer_list<int>` constructor, yielding a single element `3`. This is the classic brace-vs-paren ambiguity.

mcqs.q: For a local `int x;` (default-initialized) followed by reading `x` before any assignment, what does the standard say?
options: It is undefined behavior; the value is indeterminate and the compiler may optimize on the assumption it never happens
`x` is guaranteed to be `0` because locals are zero-initialized
It is a compile error under any conforming compiler
It is well-defined but implementation-defined to some garbage value
mcqs.explanation: A default-initialized built-in with automatic storage holds an indeterminate value, and reading it is undefined behavior. Only static/thread-duration objects are zero-initialized. `int x{};` would value-initialize it to 0.

mcqs.q: Which type trait must hold before you may safely `std::memcpy` an object?
options: `std::is_polymorphic_v<T>`
`std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>`
`std::has_virtual_destructor_v<T>`
`std::is_default_constructible_v<T>`
mcqs.explanation: `std::is_trivially_copyable` is the precise property `memcpy`/`bit_cast` need. A type with a `std::string` member is excluded because copying its bytes would duplicate an owning pointer rather than perform the deep copy the string requires.

options: `c` is `std::uint8_t` with value `44` (wraps mod 256)
`c` is `unsigned` with value `300`
`c` is `int` with value `300`
`c` is `std::uint8_t` with value `300`, which is UB
mcqs.explanation: Integer promotion lifts both `uint8_t` operands to `int` before the addition, so `a + b` is an `int` equal to `300` — it does not wrap. It would only truncate if you assigned the result back into a `uint8_t`.

mcqs.q: Why are C-style casts like `(Order*)p` banned in many HFT/style-guide codebases?
options: They are slower at runtime than the named casts
They are a syntax error in C++17 and later
They always invoke a `dynamic_cast` and pull in RTTI
They silently expand to whichever of const_cast/static_cast/reinterpret_cast compiles first, are un-greppable, and a refactor can change which
mcqs.explanation: A C-style cast tries const_cast, static_cast, static_cast+const_cast, reinterpret_cast, then reinterpret_cast+const_cast in order, using the first that compiles. You cannot tell which you got, can't grep for the dangerous ones, and a refactor can silently turn a benign static_cast into a reinterpret_cast.

mcqs.q: What is the correct, well-defined way to reinterpret a `float`'s bits as a `std::uint32_t` in C++20?
options: `std::bit_cast<std::uint32_t>(f)`
`(std::uint32_t)f`
`reinterpret_cast<std::uint32_t&>(f)`
`static_cast<std::uint32_t>(f)`
mcqs.explanation: `std::bit_cast` copies the object representation without violating strict aliasing and is `constexpr`. `reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(f)` is strict-aliasing UB; `static_cast`/the C-cast perform a value conversion (truncating 1.5f to 1), not a bit reinterpretation.

mcqs.q: Which is a leak of a plain unscoped `enum` that `enum class` fixes?
options: Unscoped enums always allocate on the heap
Enumerators implicitly convert to `int` and the names leak into the enclosing scope
Unscoped enums forbid use inside a `switch`
Unscoped enums cannot have an underlying type at all
mcqs.explanation: Unscoped `enum`s implicitly convert to `int` (so `Color == 1` compiles) and inject their enumerators into the enclosing scope (so two enums can't both have `Buy`). `enum class` removes the implicit conversion and scopes the names under the enum's name.

mcqs.q: What is the underlying type of `enum class E { A, B };` when unspecified?
options: `std::uint8_t`
`unsigned int`
`int`
Implementation-defined, chosen to fit the values
mcqs.explanation: A scoped enum's underlying type defaults to `int` when unspecified. By contrast, an unscoped enum without an explicit underlying type has an implementation-defined underlying type chosen to fit its values — a portability hazard for serialization.

mcqs.q: `static` is overloaded in C++. Which set of meanings is correct depending on where it appears?
options: Namespace scope = external linkage; function-local = automatic duration; class member = per-object
It is only valid on class members in modern C++
It always means "static storage duration" regardless of context
Namespace scope = internal linkage; function-local = static duration (no linkage); class member = one shared instance
mcqs.explanation: At namespace scope `static` gives internal linkage; inside a function it gives static storage duration with no linkage (initialized once, thread-safely since C++11); on a class member it means a single instance shared by all objects.

mcqs.q: Which attribute is the standard cure for *false sharing* between two atomics hammered by different threads?
options: `alignas(64)` (or `std::hardware_destructive_interference_size`) so each gets its own cache line
`[[likely]]` on the access branch
`thread_local` on each atomic
`[[nodiscard]]` on the accessor functions
mcqs.explanation: False sharing occurs when two independently-written variables share a 64-byte cache line, causing cache-line ping-pong. Padding each to its own line with `alignas(64)` (or `hardware_destructive_interference_size`) eliminates it.

coding.prompt: Define a POD-style wire message `struct Tick { std::int64_t ts; std::int32_t px; std::int32_t qty; };` and add `static_assert`s proving it is **trivially copyable** and **standard-layout** (so it is safe to `memcpy`/`bit_cast`). Then write `std::size_t serialize(const Tick& t, std::byte* out)` that copies a `Tick` into a caller-provided `std::byte` buffer using `std::memcpy`, returning the number of bytes written. Click **▶ Run tests** to check against the test cases.
hints: Include `<cstdint>`, `<cstddef>`, `<cstring>`, and `<type_traits>`.
The traits you want are `std::is_trivially_copyable_v` and `std::is_standard_layout_v`.
coding.discussion: Trivial copyability is exactly the precondition `std::memcpy`/`std::bit_cast` require — the bytes fully represent the value, with no owning pointers (a `std::string` member would break it). `sizeof(Tick)` is 16 here (no padding, since members are in descending-alignment order). On the wire you would still pin field widths with `<cstdint>` types and worry about endianness; trivially-copyable + standard-layout is what makes the fast copy-by-bytes path legal.

coding.prompt: Define a scoped enum `MsgType : char` with `NewOrder = 'N'`, `Cancel = 'C'`, `Execution = 'E'`. Add a `static_assert` that `sizeof(MsgType) == 1`. Write `const char* name(MsgType)` that maps each value to a string using an **exhaustive `switch` with no `default`** so a future enumerator forces a compiler warning. Also provide a C++17-compatible `to_underlying` helper. Unknown values should return `"?"`.
hints: Pin the underlying type to `char` in the enum declaration.
`std::underlying_type_t<MsgType>` gives the integer type for the cast.
coding.discussion: Pinning `: char` makes `sizeof` exactly one byte — what you want when the enum mirrors a one-byte wire tag — and lets the enum be forward-declared. Omitting `default` is deliberate: with `-Wswitch -Werror`, adding a fourth enumerator turns every unhandled `switch` into a build break instead of a silent fall-through in production. In C++23 you would use the standard `std::to_underlying` instead of the hand-rolled helper.

mcqs.q: Given `int a[4];` and `int* p = a;`, why does `p + 1` advance 4 bytes while a `char* c; c + 1` advances 1?
options: `int*` is wider than `char*`, so the pointer itself is larger
Pointer arithmetic is scaled by `sizeof(T)` of the pointee type
Pointers always advance by 1 byte; the difference is a compiler bug
The array bounds force `int*` to skip padding
mcqs.explanation: Adding `n` to a `T*` advances by `n * sizeof(T)` bytes so the result points at the next `T`. `sizeof(int)` is 4 and `sizeof(char)` is 1, which is the single rule explaining both. This is also why `void*` arithmetic is ill-formed in standard C++.

mcqs.q: Why is `f(NULL)` ambiguous (or wrong) when both `void f(int)` and `void f(int*)` exist, but `f(nullptr)` is not?
options: There is no difference; both call `f(int*)`
`nullptr` is a macro that expands to `(void*)0`
`NULL`/`0` are integer constants and prefer `f(int)`; `nullptr` has type `std::nullptr_t` that converts only to pointers
`NULL` is a keyword reserved for pointers only
mcqs.explanation: `NULL`/`0` are null pointer *constants* that are integer literals, so they match `f(int)`. `nullptr` is of type `std::nullptr_t`, which implicitly converts to any pointer type but never to an integer, so it unambiguously selects `f(int*)`.

mcqs.q: What two operations does `new T{...}` perform, and in what order?
options: It only allocates storage; the constructor runs lazily on first use
It calls `malloc` then `memset`s the bytes to zero
First the constructor runs, then `operator new` allocates storage
First `operator new` obtains raw storage, then the constructor builds the `T` object in it
mcqs.explanation: `new T{...}` calls `operator new(sizeof(T))` to get suitably-aligned raw storage (which may hit the allocator/OS), then constructs a `T` in place. `delete` is the mirror: run the destructor, then `operator delete`.

mcqs.q: Why is `delete a;` (without brackets) undefined behavior for `int* a = new int[10];`?
options: `new[]` stores element-count bookkeeping that only `delete[]` consults; plain `delete` skips it and corrupts the allocator
It is actually fine; `delete` and `delete[]` are interchangeable
`a` is `const` so it cannot be deleted
`delete` cannot free heap memory, only `free` can
mcqs.explanation: `new[]` typically stores the element count in a header so `delete[]` knows how many destructors to run and how to return the block. Calling plain `delete` skips that bookkeeping — UB. You must pair `new`/`delete` and `new[]`/`delete[]` exactly.

options: It leaks `local` because there is no matching `delete`
It returns the address of an automatic object whose lifetime ends at return; dereferencing the result is UB (dangling pointer)
It is fine; `local` is copied into the returned pointer
It is a double free
mcqs.explanation: `local` has automatic storage duration and dies when the function returns, so the returned pointer dangles and dereferencing it is undefined behavior. Returning by value, or allocating with a lifetime that outlives the call, is the fix.

mcqs.q: Which is true of `const int* p;` versus `int* const q;`?
options: Both forbid writing through the pointer
Both are identical because const binds to the pointer either way
`p` can be repointed but you cannot write through it; `q` cannot be repointed but you can write through it
`p` cannot be repointed; `q` can be repointed
mcqs.explanation: Read right-to-left: `const int* p` is a (mutable) pointer to const int — repointable, not writable-through. `int* const q` is a const pointer to (mutable) int — writable-through, not repointable. `const int*` protects the data; `int* const` protects the binding.

mcqs.q: Why is adding low-level const (`const int* r = some_int_ptr;`) allowed implicitly, but dropping it (`int* s = r;`) requires a `const_cast`?
options: It is a compiler limitation that LTO removes
Both directions are implicit; the question's premise is false
Low-level const is part of the name, not the type, so it cannot convert at all
Adding a const promise is always safe; removing it could let you write through a pointer the type system promised was read-only
mcqs.explanation: Adding low-level const only strengthens the read-only guarantee, so it is always implicit. Dropping it would silently re-enable mutation through a pointer the type said was const, so the language forces an explicit `const_cast`.

mcqs.q: Why is returning `const std::string` by value an anti-pattern?
options: The top-level const on the returned value blocks move semantics, forcing copies
It changes the function's mangled name and breaks linking
It causes a memory leak in the caller
`const` return values cannot be assigned to any variable
mcqs.explanation: A `const` prvalue cannot be moved from (the move constructor takes a non-const rvalue reference), so callers are forced to copy the result. Return a plain `std::string` so the result can be moved or elided.

mcqs.q: Why does a lambda passed to a function *template* inline, while the same lambda stored in a `std::function` does not?
options: `std::function` disables optimization globally
The template preserves the lambda's concrete type so the call is direct; `std::function` type-erases it into an indirect call the optimizer can't see through
Templates copy the lambda's body textually into the caller
Lambdas in templates are always `constexpr`
mcqs.explanation: When the callable's concrete type is a template parameter, `op(args)` is a direct call the optimizer flattens. `std::function` erases the type behind a vtable-like dispatch, producing an indirect call (and possibly a heap allocation) that defeats inlining.

mcqs.q: Under what condition can a lambda be implicitly converted to a plain function pointer?
options: Only when it is marked `mutable`
Never; lambdas are always closure objects
Only when it is captureless (stateless)
Whenever it captures exactly one variable by value
mcqs.explanation: A captureless lambda has no state, so the standard makes it convertible to a function pointer of the matching signature — handy for C APIs. A capturing lambda carries state with nowhere to live in a bare function pointer, so no such conversion exists.

mcqs.q: Which statement about `std::function` is TRUE?
options: It guarantees the same machine code as a templated callable parameter
It never allocates and always inlines through the call
It can only hold lambdas, not free functions or functors
It may heap-allocate when the wrapped callable's state exceeds its small-buffer size, and each call is an indirect call
mcqs.explanation: `std::function` stores the callable in a small inline buffer; if the captured state is larger than that buffer it silently heap-allocates. Calls dispatch through an internal vtable-like mechanism — an indirect call the compiler generally cannot inline.

coding.prompt: Without using `<algorithm>` or any STL container, write `void copy_array(const int* src, int* dst, std::size_t n)` that copies `n` ints from `src` to `dst` using only pointer arithmetic (no indexing with `[]`). Assume the ranges do not overlap.
hints: Walk a `const int*` over the source and an `int*` over the destination.
`*dst++ = *src++;` advances both pointers while assigning.
coding.discussion: `*dst++ = *src++` dereferences then post-increments both pointers; pointer arithmetic is scaled by `sizeof(int)` so each `++` steps a full element. Forming `src + n` (one-past-the-end) is legal as long as you do not dereference it. Complexity is O(n) with one load and one store per element. For overlapping ranges you would need `std::memmove` semantics; here non-overlap is assumed (like `memcpy`).

coding.prompt: Write `void reverse_in_place(int* a, std::size_t n)` that reverses an array of `n` ints in place using two pointers walking toward each other (no extra array, no `[]` indexing).
hints: Use a `left` pointer at the start and a `right` pointer at `a + n - 1`.
Swap `*left` and `*right`, then move `left` forward and `right` backward until they meet or cross.
coding.discussion: Two pointers converge from the ends, swapping pairs — O(n) time, O(1) extra space, with n/2 swaps. The `n == 0` guard matters: computing `a + n - 1` when `n == 0` would form an invalid pointer (before the array). Using `left < right` rather than `!=` keeps the loop correct for both even and odd `n`. This is the canonical in-place reversal pattern.

mcqs.q: For `template <class T> void f(T&& p);`, what is `T` when called as `f(x)` where `x` is an lvalue `int`?
options: `T` is deduced as `int&` (an lvalue reference), and reference collapsing makes the parameter `int&`
Deduction fails because `x` is not an rvalue
`T` is `const int` and the parameter is `const int&`
`T` is `int` and the parameter is `int&&`
mcqs.explanation: `T&&` is a forwarding reference: for an lvalue argument, `T` is deduced as an lvalue reference (`int&`), then `int& &&` collapses to `int&`. For an rvalue, `T` would be `int` and the parameter `int&&`. This category-dependence is what makes `std::forward` work.

mcqs.q: What is the type of `x` in `auto x{42};` under C++17, and what was it before?
options: `int` in both
`int` in C++17; `std::initializer_list<int>` before
`std::initializer_list<int>` in both
`std::initializer_list<int>` in C++17; `int` before
mcqs.explanation: C++17 (via N3922) made `auto x{42};` deduce `int` for a single-element braced-init. Before, it deduced `std::initializer_list<int>`. Note `auto x = {42};` is *still* an `initializer_list` — the copy-list-init form.

mcqs.q: Given `int x = 0;`, what are `decltype(x)` and `decltype((x))`?
options: `int` and `int` respectively
`int&` and `int&` respectively
`int` and `int&` respectively
`const int` and `int&`
mcqs.explanation: `decltype` of a bare name yields the declared type `int`. But `(x)` is a parenthesized lvalue *expression* (not a name), and `decltype` adds an `&` for non-name lvalue expressions, giving `int&`. This is the famous extra `decltype` rule.

mcqs.q: Why is `int z = square(2);` NOT guaranteed to be evaluated at compile time, while `constexpr int z = square(2);` is?
options: `constexpr` functions can only ever run at compile time
Plain `int` cannot hold a compile-time value
`square(2)` is too complex to evaluate at compile time
`constexpr` evaluation is forced only in a constant-evaluated context; a plain initializer is not one (though the optimizer may still fold it)
mcqs.explanation: A `constexpr` function runs at compile time only in a constant-evaluated context (constexpr-var init, `static_assert`, array bound, template arg). `int z = square(2);` is not such a context, so the standard does not require it — though optimizers fold it at `-O1+`. Naming a `constexpr` variable forces it.

mcqs.q: Which one-sentence distinction is correct?
options: `const` = read-only; `constexpr` = may be compile-time; `consteval` = must be compile-time; `constinit` = constant-initialized but mutable
`const` and `constexpr` are synonyms; `consteval` allows runtime calls; `constinit` makes objects immutable
`constexpr` = read-only; `const` = compile-time; `consteval` = optional compile-time; `constinit` = thread-local
All four guarantee compile-time evaluation
mcqs.explanation: `const` means read-only (value may be runtime-computed). `constexpr` permits compile-time evaluation. `consteval` (immediate function) requires it on every call. `constinit` guarantees constant initialization (no dynamic-init fiasco) but the object stays mutable.

mcqs.q: Why does `typename T::value_type x;` require the `typename` keyword inside a template?
options: `typename` forces a heap allocation of `x`
`T::value_type` is a dependent name and the compiler assumes it is a value unless `typename` says it is a type
Without it the variable would have static storage duration
`typename` is just a style alias for `class` and is optional here
mcqs.explanation: In phase-1 of two-phase lookup, a dependent name like `T::value_type` could be a type or a value, and the compiler defaults to assuming a *value*. `typename` disambiguates it as a type. The same need motivates the `template` disambiguator for dependent member templates.

mcqs.q: How many distinct functions does `add(1, 2); add(1.0, 2.0);` put in the binary for `template <class T> T add(T a, T b);`, and why?
options: Three — one for each call site plus the primary template
One — the compiler shares a single generic body
Two — templates are monomorphized: one full machine-code copy per distinct type argument
Zero — templates only generate code when explicitly instantiated
mcqs.explanation: Templates are monomorphized: `add<int>` and `add<double>` are two separate functions (an integer add vs an FPU add). This is why templates are fast (everything concrete and inlinable) and why they bloat binary size and build time.

mcqs.q: Which can be *partially* specialized?
options: All three: class, function, and variable templates
Only function templates and class templates
Function templates only
Class templates and variable templates, but NOT function templates
mcqs.explanation: Partial specialization is allowed for class templates and variable templates but forbidden for function templates. To get partial-specialization-like behavior for functions you use overloading, which supports patterns and participates in overload resolution.

mcqs.q: What does SFINAE stand for, and how does `std::enable_if` exploit it?
options: Substitution Failure Is Not An Error — if substituting a template argument makes a signature ill-formed, that overload is silently removed rather than causing a hard error
Substitution Forces Immediate Named Evaluation — it forces compile-time evaluation
Simple Function Interface Negotiation And Evaluation — it picks the fastest overload
Static Function Inlining And Name Erasure — it inlines templates aggressively
mcqs.explanation: SFINAE = Substitution Failure Is Not An Error. When `enable_if_t<cond>` has no `::type` because the condition is false, substitution fails and that overload is quietly dropped from the overload set, letting another candidate win. `if constexpr` and concepts are the modern replacements for most uses.

options: `std::function` cannot hold a capturing lambda
`[&]` captures `local` by reference; `local` dies when `make_bad` returns, so the returned closure dangles (UB)
The lambda must be marked `mutable` to compile
`use(local)` copies `local`, so this is fine
mcqs.explanation: `[&]` stores a reference to `local`, whose lifetime ends when `make_bad` returns. The escaping closure then references a destroyed object — a dangling-capture bug. Capture by value (`[local]`) or by init-capture/`*this` when a closure outlives its source.

mcqs.q: Why must `[n = 0]() mutable { return ++n; }` be marked `mutable`?
options: `mutable` is required for any init-capture
Without `mutable` the lambda would heap-allocate
A lambda's `operator()` is `const` by default, so modifying the by-value capture `n` requires `mutable`
`mutable` makes the capture by reference instead of by value
mcqs.explanation: The closure's `operator()` is `const` unless declared `mutable`. Since `n` is a by-value capture (a data member of the closure), mutating it inside the call operator needs `mutable`. By-reference captures modify the referent regardless of `mutable`.

coding.prompt: Write a single function template `T max3(const T& a, const T& b, const T& c)` that returns the largest of three values of the same type `T`, requiring only that `T` supports `operator<` (or `>`). It must work for any orderable type (the tests instantiate it with `int`, `double`, and `char`).
hints: Deduce `T` from the arguments; no explicit template arguments needed.
Compute the max of the first two, then compare against the third.
coding.discussion: The compiler deduces `T` from the arguments and stamps out one concrete function per distinct `T` (monomorphization), so `max3<int>` and `max3<double>` are two functions in the object file. Taking `const T&` avoids copying for expensive types; returning by value avoids dangling. The only requirement on `T` is a usable `>` — instantiate it with a type lacking that and you get an error only at the point of use (on-demand member instantiation).

coding.prompt: Using C++14 `constexpr` features, write a `constexpr` function `unsigned long long factorial(unsigned n)` that uses a loop (not recursion). Add a `static_assert` proving `factorial(10) == 3628800` is computed at compile time. The tests check it both at compile time and at runtime.
hints: C++14 allows loops and local mutation inside a `constexpr` function.
Use a `static_assert` to force constant evaluation.
coding.discussion: C++11 `constexpr` was effectively a single `return` (no loops/local mutation); C++14 relaxed this to allow loops, multiple statements, and mutation of locals — which is why this body is legal. The `static_assert` is a constant-evaluated context, so the loop runs in the *compiler* and the result is baked in. The same definition still works as an ordinary runtime call when given a non-constant argument.

coding.prompt: Write a generic `template <class T> void serialize(std::byte* out, const T& v)` that uses **`if constexpr`** to pick a fast path for trivially-copyable types (a `std::memcpy`) and a slow path otherwise (calls `v.serialize(out)`). Explain why `if constexpr` is preferable to tag-dispatch or `enable_if` here. The tests call it with a trivial struct and with a class that provides its own `serialize`.
hints: Include `<type_traits>`, `<cstddef>`, `<cstring>`.
`if constexpr (std::is_trivially_copyable_v<T>) { ... } else { ... }`
coding.discussion: `if constexpr` discards the untaken branch *before* it is type-checked for instantiation, so the `memcpy` branch never has to be valid for a non-trivial `T` and vice versa. Compared with tag dispatch (`std::true_type`/`std::false_type` overloads) or `enable_if`, this is one function, one place to read, with crisp errors and no overload-set surprises (notably the Sutter pitfall where a function-template specialization attaches to the wrong base). The chosen path is the only one emitted — zero runtime cost.

mcqs.q: Why is `std::string_view sv = std::string("hi");` a bug?
options: `string_view` cannot be constructed from a `std::string`
It fails to compile because of an ambiguous conversion
`string_view` always copies, so this wastes an allocation
The temporary `std::string` is destroyed at the end of the statement, leaving `sv` viewing freed memory (use-after-free)
mcqs.explanation: `string_view` is a non-owning {ptr, len}. The temporary `std::string` it points into dies at the semicolon, so `sv` dangles. Never store/return a `string_view` that outlives its source buffer.

mcqs.q: When would you choose `std::variant<Ts...>` + `std::visit` over a virtual base class?
options: When the set of types is closed/known at compile time and you want stack storage, no heap, and compiler-checked exhaustive dispatch
When you need each object to be heap-allocated for stable addresses
When new types may be loaded at runtime as plugins
When you cannot enumerate the alternatives in advance
mcqs.explanation: `variant` shines for a closed set known at compile time: it stores the value inline (no heap), needs no RTTI, and `std::visit` is exhaustively checked. An open, runtime-extensible set (plugins) is where inheritance/`std::any` earn their place.

mcqs.q: What are the data members of `std::array<int, 4>`, and what is its `sizeof`?
options: A pointer to a heap buffer; `sizeof` is 8
A single C array `int[4]` and nothing else; `sizeof` is 16
Four separate `int` fields plus a length; `sizeof` is 20
A pointer, size, and capacity; `sizeof` is 24
mcqs.explanation: `std::array<T,N>` is a thin aggregate wrapping exactly a `T[N]` — no pointer, no size field, no capacity, no allocator. `sizeof(std::array<int,4>)` is `4 * sizeof(int)` = 16, identical to the C array.

mcqs.q: Why does a *non-`noexcept`* move constructor make `std::vector` growth slower?
options: It forces the growth factor down from 2 to 1, making pushes O(n^2)
The vector cannot move at all without `noexcept`, so it leaks
To preserve its strong exception guarantee, the vector copies elements on reallocation unless the move constructor is `noexcept`
Non-`noexcept` moves disable inlining of the whole vector
mcqs.explanation: On reallocation the vector uses `std::move_if_noexcept`: if `T`'s move could throw mid-transfer it cannot restore the strong guarantee, so it falls back to copying. Marking moves `noexcept` lets it move (cheap) instead of copy — a common hidden performance cliff.

options: Always a use-after-free regardless of capacity
It is a compile error to take `&v[0]`
Always safe; `p` tracks the element across reallocation
If the `push_back` reallocates, `p` dangles and `use(*p)` is a use-after-free
mcqs.explanation: A reallocating `push_back` moves all elements to a new buffer and frees the old one, invalidating every pointer/iterator/reference — so `p` dangles. The fix is to `reserve` enough capacity up front (so no reallocation happens) or store an index instead of a pointer.

mcqs.q: Why is `n` `push_back`s on an empty vector total O(n), not O(n^2)?
options: The vector grows geometrically (e.g. x1.5 or x2), so total copy work is a geometric series that sums to O(n) — amortized O(1) per push
`push_back` reserves all memory on the first call
The compiler caches the vector's size, avoiding recomputation
Each `push_back` is always O(1) because the buffer never moves
mcqs.explanation: Capacity grows by a constant factor on each reallocation, so the summed cost of all the move/copy work across n pushes is a geometric series equal to O(n). Hence each `push_back` is amortized O(1), even though an individual grow is O(size).

mcqs.q: Which single operation does `std::list` do in O(1) that `std::vector` genuinely cannot?
options: Reserving capacity up front to avoid reallocation
`splice` — moving a range of nodes between lists by pointer relinking, with no element copies
Random access via `operator[]`
Contiguous `memcpy` of all elements to a C API
mcqs.explanation: `splice` relinks node pointers to transplant elements between lists in O(1) without moving or copying them — unique to linked structures. `vector` has no equivalent. (Note even `list` insert/erase is O(1) only *given an iterator*; reaching position k is O(k).)

mcqs.q: On libstdc++/libc++, which integer-key distribution turns `std::unordered_map<int, V>` average O(1) into effectively O(n)?
options: Keys that are negative
Keys that are all distinct large primes
Keys that collide into few buckets because `std::hash<int>` is the identity and `% bucket_count` maps them together
Keys inserted after calling `reserve`
mcqs.explanation: `std::hash<int>` is the identity in libstdc++/libc++, so a poor key distribution (combined with `% bucket_count`) can pile keys into a handful of buckets, lengthening chains to O(n). Mixing the key bits or using a table that hashes internally avoids this.

mcqs.q: What does `reserve(n)` on a `std::unordered_map` allocate?
options: Nothing; `unordered_map` has no `reserve`
It allocates one contiguous block holding all n key/value pairs
It constructs n default value nodes immediately
It sizes the bucket array for n elements (avoiding rehash) but does NOT pre-allocate the per-element nodes
mcqs.explanation: `reserve(n)` ensures the bucket array is large enough to hold n elements without rehashing, but the nodes are still allocated one-per-insert. It is the key call to avoid mid-burst rehash spikes (a rehash is an O(n) reallocation + redistribution).

mcqs.q: A colleague writes `bool operator()(int a, int b) const { return a <= b; }` as a `std::map` comparator. What goes wrong?
options: `<=` is not irreflexive, so it violates strict weak ordering — undefined behavior (corrupted tree, crashes, infinite loops)
It only sorts descending instead of ascending
It makes lookups O(n) but is otherwise safe
Nothing; `<=` is a valid comparator
mcqs.explanation: An ordered container's `Compare` must be a strict weak ordering: irreflexive (`comp(a,a)` is false), asymmetric, transitive. `<=` gives `comp(a,a) == true`, breaking irreflexivity — which is UB, not merely a wrong sort order.

mcqs.q: Why does `std::map` guarantee O(log n) *worst case* while `std::unordered_map` only guarantees it *amortized average*?
options: `std::map` caches all results, so it is always O(1)
`std::map` is a balanced (red-black) tree with bounded height; `unordered_map` degrades to O(n) under collisions and pays O(n) rehash spikes
Both guarantee the same complexity; the premise is false
`unordered_map` is always faster, so the guarantee does not matter
mcqs.explanation: `std::map` uses a self-balancing BST whose height is bounded by ~2*log2(n+1), giving O(log n) worst case. A hash map is average O(1) but worst case O(n) (all keys collide) and suffers occasional O(n) rehashes, so only amortized-average bounds hold.

mcqs.q: Is `std::deque` contiguous, and does it have a `.data()` member?
options: Yes and yes — like `std::vector` it is one contiguous block
It is contiguous but intentionally hides `.data()`
No and no — it stores elements in separately-allocated chunks linked by a map, so there is no single flat buffer
It is non-contiguous but still provides `.data()` for the first chunk
mcqs.explanation: A deque is segmented: fixed-size chunks tracked by a map (array of chunk pointers). Elements are contiguous *within* a chunk but not across the whole container, so there is no `.data()` and you cannot hand it to a C API expecting a flat buffer.

mcqs.q: After `d.push_back(x)` on a `std::deque`, which stays valid?
options: Both pointers/references and iterators are invalidated
Only iterators stay valid; pointers/references dangle
Both pointers/references and iterators stay valid
Pointers/references to existing elements stay valid, but all iterators are invalidated
mcqs.explanation: End insertion on a deque keeps pointers/references stable (elements never move; a new chunk is linked in) but invalidates all iterators (which must track position in the map). This is the inverse of `std::vector`, where a reallocating `push_back` invalidates both.

mcqs.q: Why can `std::stack` be backed by `std::vector` but `std::queue` cannot?
options: `queue` needs `pop_front`, which `std::vector` lacks; `stack` only needs `back`/`push_back`/`pop_back`, which `vector` has
`stack` requires `pop_front`, which only `vector` provides
`vector` is too slow to back a queue
`queue` requires a node-based container by the standard
mcqs.explanation: `std::queue` requires `front`, `back`, `push_back`, and `pop_front`; `std::vector` has no `pop_front`, so it won't compile as a queue's backing. `std::stack` needs only `back`/`push_back`/`pop_back`, all of which `vector` provides (and contiguity often makes it faster).

mcqs.q: You want a `std::priority_queue` that always yields the *smallest* element first. Which comparator do you pass, and why?
options: No comparator works; `priority_queue` is always a max-heap
`std::greater` — top() is the element greatest under Compare, and under `greater` the smallest value is the greatest, giving a min-heap
`std::less` — it naturally produces a min-heap
`std::equal_to` — it orders by equality
mcqs.explanation: `priority_queue` puts the element *greatest* under `Compare` on top. The default `std::less` makes the largest value greatest (a max-heap). Passing `std::greater` reverses the ordering so the smallest value is 'greatest', producing a min-heap — the usual choice for earliest-deadline-first scheduling.

coding.prompt: Write `void remove_zeros(std::vector<int>& v)` that removes every element equal to `0` in a single O(n) pass using the **erase-remove idiom**. (The relative order of the surviving elements must be preserved.) The discussion shows the C++20 one-line equivalent.
hints: `std::remove` shuffles kept elements to the front and returns the new logical end.
`v.erase(first, v.end())` drops the unspecified tail. C++20 has `std::erase`.
coding.discussion: `std::remove` does not actually erase — it moves the kept elements forward and returns an iterator to the new logical end, leaving the tail unspecified; `vector::erase` then drops that tail. The whole thing is one O(n) pass with no per-element shifting (unlike erasing in a loop, which is O(n^2)). C++20's free `std::erase`/`std::erase_if` collapse the two-iterator dance to one call.

coding.prompt: Using `std::priority_queue` as a **min-heap**, write `std::vector<long> drain_sorted(std::vector<long> timestamps)` that pushes every timestamp onto the heap and then pops them into a result vector in **ascending** order (earliest first). Use `long` timestamps. Read `top()` before `pop()` since `pop()` returns `void`.
hints: A min-heap is `std::priority_queue<long, std::vector<long>, std::greater<long>>`.
Read `top()` first, then `pop()` — `pop()` returns `void`.
coding.discussion: `std::greater` flips the ordering so the smallest timestamp is 'greatest' under Compare and lands on top — a min-heap, the standard discrete-event-scheduling structure. `push`/`pop` are O(log n), `top` is O(1). Note `pop()` returns `void` (you must read `top()` first), and a `priority_queue` exposes no iteration or search — only top/push/pop. For HFT you would often prefer a flat array/ring buffer, but a binary heap is the textbook scheduler.

coding.prompt: Given a sorted `std::vector<std::pair<int,double>>` keyed ascending by `.first`, write `std::optional<double> find_price(const std::vector<std::pair<int,double>>& book, int key)` that returns the matching value using `std::lower_bound` (O(log n)), or `std::nullopt` if the key is absent. Explain why a sorted vector can beat `std::map` here.
hints: Pass a comparator projecting the pair's `.first`.
Check the returned iterator is not `end()` and its key matches before returning the value.
coding.discussion: `std::lower_bound` does an O(log n) binary search over contiguous memory, so the hot upper levels of the search stay cache-resident and each step walks one cache line — versus `std::map`, which scatters nodes across the heap so each of the log n hops is a fresh cache miss. The trade is that inserting into a sorted vector is O(n) (shift), so this wins for *read-mostly* data (build once, query often). C++23's `std::flat_map` standardizes exactly this idea.

mcqs.q: What is the ONLY language-level difference between `struct` and `class` in C++?
options: `struct` cannot use inheritance or templates
`struct` cannot have member functions or constructors
Default member access (and default inheritance): `public` for `struct`, `private` for `class`
`class` generates faster code than `struct`
mcqs.explanation: `struct` and `class` are the same feature; they differ only in defaults — members and base classes are `public` by default in a `struct`, `private` in a `class`. Anyone claiming `struct` is 'faster' is confused; the generated code is identical.

mcqs.q:
What is `sizeof` this struct on a typical x86-64 ABI?

```cpp
struct S { char a; double b; int c; char d; };
```
options: 16 — the compiler reorders fields automatically
32 — every member is padded to 8 bytes
14 — the exact sum of member sizes with no padding
24 — padding aligns `b` to 8 and the struct rounds up to a multiple of its 8-byte alignment
mcqs.explanation: Members lay out in declaration order with padding to satisfy alignment: `a`(0), 7 pad, `b`(8), `c`(16), `d`(20), then 3 tail-pad to round to a multiple of 8 -> 24. Reordering to descending alignment (double, int, char, char) would shrink it to 16.

mcqs.q: Why is `sizeof(EmptyClass) == 1` rather than 0?
options: The standard requires distinct objects to have distinct addresses, which a zero-size object in an array could not provide
Alignment rounds 0 up to the nearest byte arbitrarily
An empty class secretly stores a vtable pointer
Every class carries a hidden 1-byte type tag
mcqs.explanation: A most-derived object must have a unique address; a zero-size object couldn't be distinguished from its neighbor in an array, so the minimum is 1 byte. As a *base* class an empty type can occupy zero bytes (Empty Base Optimization / C++20 `[[no_unique_address]]`).

mcqs.q: Members are initialized in which order?
options: Reverse declaration order
Declaration order in the class, regardless of the order written in the initializer list
The order written in the initializer list
Alphabetical by member name
mcqs.explanation: Members always initialize in declaration order, not the order they appear in the initializer list. If a member's initializer reads another member and the orders disagree, you get a use-before-init bug — which `-Wreorder` warns about.

mcqs.q: For a `std::string` member, what extra work does `name_ = n;` in the constructor body do compared to `: name_(n)` in the initializer list?
options: Nothing; both forms generate identical code for all member types
It moves `n` instead of copying, which is faster
It default-constructs `name_` first, then copy-assigns over it — an extra construct/allocate the list avoids
It leaks the string's buffer
mcqs.explanation: By the time the body runs, every member is already constructed. So `name_ = n;` runs the default constructor then copy-assignment (which may free the just-allocated empty buffer and allocate again). The initializer list runs a single copy constructor — one allocation instead of two operations.

mcqs.q: A function takes `Order` by value and a `std::vector<Order>` stores them. Passing an `IcebergOrder` (derived) loses its `hidden_qty`. What is this called and what is the fix?
options: A double free; add a copy constructor
Type erasure; wrap it in `std::any`
A dangling reference; mark the destructor `virtual`
Object slicing; pass/store by reference or pointer (e.g. `std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Order>>`)
mcqs.explanation: Copying a derived object into a base by value copies only the base subobject and silently drops the derived members — object slicing. Pass polymorphic types by reference/pointer and store them as `std::unique_ptr<Base>` (or use a variant) to avoid it.

mcqs.q: Why is `delete basePtr;` undefined behavior when `~Base` is non-virtual but the object is really a `Derived`?
options: Without a virtual destructor the runtime calls only `~Base`, so `~Derived` never runs and the derived part leaks/corrupts
Deleting through a base pointer is always UB regardless of the destructor
It throws `std::bad_cast` at runtime
`delete` cannot be applied to base pointers at all
mcqs.explanation: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer with a non-virtual destructor is UB; in practice `~Derived` is never invoked, leaking whatever it owned. A class meant to be deleted polymorphically needs a `virtual` destructor (if it's never deleted that way, non-virtual is fine and cheaper).

mcqs.q: In a two-level hierarchy `D : B`, what is the construction/destruction order?
options: Order is unspecified
Construct: base then derived members (declaration order) then derived body; destruction is the exact reverse
Construct: derived first, then base; destruction in the same order
Both construction and destruction go base-first
mcqs.explanation: Construction is base subobject(s), then members in declaration order, then the derived constructor body. Destruction runs in the exact reverse: derived body, members (reverse declaration order), then the base destructor.

mcqs.q: You add a user-declared `~T()` to a class that previously declared none. What happens to its move constructor?
options: The copy constructor is deleted instead
Nothing changes; moves are always generated
The move operations are NOT generated, so the type silently falls back to copying
The move constructor is deleted, causing a compile error on any move
mcqs.explanation: Declaring a destructor (or any copy operation) suppresses implicit generation of the move operations. The type then *copies* where you expected a move — a silent performance bug. This motivates the Rule of Five: if you write one of dtor/copy/move, decide all five.

mcqs.q: Why is `explicit operator bool()` preferred over `operator int()` for a validity check?
options: `operator int()` is illegal in modern C++
`operator bool()` cannot be called inside an `if` at all
`explicit` makes the conversion run at compile time
`explicit` blocks accidental implicit conversions to integers while still working in `if`/`while` via contextual conversion
mcqs.explanation: An implicit `operator int()` invites bugs (the object silently becomes an int in arithmetic, comparisons, etc.). `explicit operator bool()` forbids those implicit conversions yet still participates in boolean contexts (`if (h)`) via contextual conversion.

mcqs.q: Why should binary `operator+` be a free (non-member) function while `operator+=` is a member?
options: A free `operator+` treats both operands symmetrically, allowing implicit conversions on the left operand too; `+=` mutates `*this` so its left operand must be the class
Free functions are always faster than members
Member `operator+` is illegal in C++
`+=` cannot be a member; it must be free
mcqs.explanation: A member `operator+` can't apply a conversion to its left operand (you can't call a member on a non-class left side), so `5 + price` wouldn't work. A free function treats both operands equally. `+=` modifies the object, so its left operand is `*this` and it must be a member.

mcqs.q: Which operators should you NOT overload, and why?
options: `==` and `<` — they break with `std::sort`
`&&`, `||`, and `,` — overloading them silently destroys short-circuit (`&&`/`||`) and sequencing (`,`) guarantees
`[]` and `()` — they must be free functions
`+`, `-`, `*` — they change operator precedence
mcqs.explanation: You technically *can* overload `&&`, `||`, and `,`, but you shouldn't: an overloaded operator is an ordinary function call that evaluates all its operands, so you lose short-circuit evaluation for `&&`/`||` and the sequencing guarantee for the comma operator.

coding.prompt: Write a move-only resource type `Engine` that owns an `int* data_` of length `n_`. Provide `explicit Engine(std::size_t n)` (zero-initialized buffer), a destructor, a `noexcept` move constructor and move assignment, and explicitly `=delete` the copy operations. Also expose `std::size_t size() const`, `int& at(std::size_t)` / `int at(std::size_t) const`, and `bool moved_from() const` (true iff the internal pointer is null). Explain why `noexcept` on the moves matters.
hints: Steal the source's pointer in the move, then null it so the source is destructible.
Copy ctor and copy assignment should be `= delete`.
coding.discussion: Declaring any move operation deletes the implicit copies, so this is move-only like `std::unique_ptr`; the explicit `=delete`s document intent. The `noexcept` on the moves is load-bearing: `std::vector<Engine>` calls `std::move_if_noexcept` on reallocation and will only *move* (an O(1) pointer steal) instead of falling back to copying if the move is `noexcept`. The move-assignment self-check and `delete[]` of the existing buffer prevent leaks and self-move corruption. A cleaner real-world design would hold the buffer in a `std::unique_ptr<int[]>` (Rule of Zero) and write none of these.

coding.prompt: Define a cheap value type `struct Price { long ticks = 0; };`. Implement `operator+=` as a member and binary `operator+` as a free function defined in terms of `+=`. Add C++20 `operator<=>` and `operator==` (both `= default`) so `Price` works in `std::set`/`std::sort`. State the ordering category you get.
hints: Binary `operator+` should take `lhs` by value, do `lhs += rhs`, and return `lhs`.
Include `<compare>` for `operator<=>`.
coding.discussion: Implementing `+` in terms of `+=` guarantees `a + b` and `a += b` agree and avoids duplicated logic; taking `lhs` by value lets the function reuse that copy as the result with no extra temporary, and for a one-`long` type it inlines to a single `add`. Because `ticks` is an integer, the defaulted `operator<=>` yields `std::strong_ordering` — a total order suitable for `std::set`/`std::map`/`std::sort`. (If `Price` wrapped a `double`, you'd get `partial_ordering` because of `NaN`, which is *not* a strict weak ordering — a reason to keep prices as integer ticks.) Binary `+` must return by value, never by reference, to avoid dangling.

mcqs.q: Given `using Price = std::int64_t; using Qty = std::int64_t;`, does `Price p = some_qty;` compile, and why is that significant?
options: Yes, but only with an explicit cast
No, the compiler rejects mixing `Price` and `Qty`
Yes, it compiles silently — `Price` and `Qty` are the same type, so a plain alias gives no type safety
No, aliases cannot be assigned to each other
mcqs.explanation: A type alias is a second *name* for the same type, not a new type. `Price` and `Qty` are both `int64_t`, so cross-assignment is legal and silent. For machine-enforced safety you need a distinct (strong) type — a tagged one-field struct.

mcqs.q: Why can `using` express `template <class T> using Vec = std::vector<T>;` but `typedef` cannot?
options: `typedef` only works inside classes
They are equivalent; the premise is false
`typedef` was removed in C++11
`using` supports alias templates (parameterized aliases); a `typedef` is a single fixed synonym with no way to bind template parameters
mcqs.explanation: The decisive advantage of `using` is the alias template — a parameterized alias. A `typedef` introduces one fixed synonym for one fixed type with no syntax to take template parameters, so `Vec<T>` is impossible to express directly with `typedef`.

mcqs.q: In the strong-type pattern `template <class T, class Tag> struct Strong;`, what is the `Tag` parameter for?
options: It makes otherwise-identical instantiations distinct types (e.g. `Strong<int64_t, PriceTag>` != `Strong<int64_t, QtyTag>`) at zero runtime cost
It enables heap allocation of the value
It stores extra runtime metadata about the value
It forces the value to be `const`
mcqs.explanation: Two instantiations differing only in `Tag` are different types even though they share the same layout (a single `int64_t`), so the compiler rejects mixing a price with a quantity. The wrapper stays standard-layout and trivially copyable — same size/alignment as the bare integer, zero runtime cost.

mcqs.q: In the zero-cost (Itanium) exception model, what is the runtime cost of *entering* a `try` block when nothing throws?
options: A constant per-`try` setup that pushes a handler frame
Zero — no extra instructions are emitted on the no-throw path; the unwind info lives in static side tables
A heap allocation for the exception machinery
Proportional to the number of destructors in scope
mcqs.explanation: The zero-cost model emits no per-`try` setup; the 'which destructors to run if an exception passes through' info lives in static tables (.gcc_except_table / LSDA). All the cost is moved onto the throw path, which is expensive and unpredictable — fine for rare errors, poison for control flow.

mcqs.q: What happens if an exception tries to escape a `noexcept` function?
options: It propagates to the caller as usual
It is automatically rethrown as a `std::bad_exception`
`std::terminate` is called immediately — there is no unwinding past the boundary and no chance to catch it higher up
It is silently swallowed and the function returns normally
mcqs.explanation: `noexcept` is a hard promise: an escaping exception calls `std::terminate` immediately, killing the process. `noexcept` does not mean 'no exceptions thrown inside' — it means none *escape*. It also shrinks caller code and enables move-on-grow in `std::vector`.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct exception-throwing/catching discipline?
options: Throw by value, catch by value, rethrow with `throw e;`
Throw by reference, catch by pointer, never rethrow
Throw by pointer, catch by value, rethrow with `throw e;`
Throw by value, catch by `const&`, and rethrow with a bare `throw;`
mcqs.explanation: Throw by value and catch by `const&` to avoid slicing polymorphic exception types. Use a bare `throw;` to rethrow the *same* object unchanged; `throw e;` would copy (and possibly slice) it. Destructors must be `noexcept` and never throw.

mcqs.q: Is `dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)` an O(1) operation?
options: No — it calls `__dynamic_cast`, which walks the base-class graph; cost grows with hierarchy depth/complexity
Yes — it is a single vtable index lookup
Yes — the compiler resolves it entirely at compile time
No — it is always exactly two memory loads
mcqs.explanation: The common wrong answer is 'it's a vtable lookup, so O(1).' In fact `dynamic_cast` is an out-of-line call to `__dynamic_cast`, which structurally walks the recorded base-class metadata to prove the relationship — not constant time, and worse with multiple/virtual inheritance. Keep it off the hot path.

mcqs.q: How do the pointer and reference forms of `dynamic_cast` report a failed cast?
options: Both return `nullptr`
Pointer form returns `nullptr`; reference form throws `std::bad_cast`
Pointer form throws; reference form returns a default object
Both throw `std::bad_cast`
mcqs.explanation: The pointer form returns `nullptr` on failure (the idiomatic `if (auto* d = dynamic_cast<D*>(b))`). The reference form can't return a null reference, so it throws `std::bad_cast` — which drags in the exception machinery, making it doubly unsuitable for a hot path.

mcqs.q: Why does `dynamic_cast<Derived*>(base)` fail to compile if `Base` has no virtual functions?
options: Non-virtual classes are always standard-layout, which `dynamic_cast` forbids
`dynamic_cast` only works on fundamental types
The down/cross-cast form requires a polymorphic source type (>=1 virtual function) so the object has a vtable carrying its `type_info`
It would compile but always return `nullptr`
mcqs.explanation: `dynamic_cast`'s downcast/cross-cast form needs the source to be polymorphic (at least one virtual function, usually a virtual destructor). The virtual function gives the object a vtable, which is where the runtime finds the `type_info` it needs to navigate the hierarchy.

mcqs.q: Why can storing a large struct in `std::any` cause a heap allocation, and what sometimes avoids it?
options: It allocates only when the type lacks a virtual destructor
`any` never allocates; it only stores a pointer to the original object
`any` always heap-allocates regardless of size
`any` keeps small/trivially-movable values inline via the Small Buffer Optimization but heap-allocates larger/non-trivial ones
mcqs.explanation: `std::any` applies a Small Buffer Optimization: small, trivially-movable values live inline in the `any` object, but anything larger (or with a non-trivial move) is heap-allocated. Combined with RTTI type checks on every access, this makes `any` a poor fit for the hot path.

mcqs.q: How does `std::variant` track which alternative is active, and why does it never heap-allocate?
options: It stores a small integer discriminant (the index) and keeps the value inline; its size is ~max(alternatives) + discriminant
It stores a vtable pointer and the active object on the heap
It uses RTTI `type_info` and stores each alternative on the heap
It hashes the type name to pick the active member
mcqs.explanation: `std::variant` is a tagged union: a `union` of the alternatives plus a small integer index recording which one is active. The value lives inline (stack/array/member), so it never allocates; `sizeof` is roughly the largest alternative plus the discriminant, rounded for alignment.

mcqs.q: When is `typeid(expr)` evaluated at runtime versus compile time?
options: Always at runtime
Runtime for a polymorphic lvalue (yields the dynamic type via the vtable); compile time for a type-id or a non-polymorphic expression
Runtime only when `-fno-rtti` is set
Always at compile time
mcqs.explanation: For a polymorphic lvalue, `typeid` reads the object's actual most-derived type at runtime via the `type_info` in its vtable. For a type operand or a non-polymorphic expression it is resolved at compile time from the static type. `typeid(*p)` on a null polymorphic `p` throws `std::bad_typeid`.

coding.prompt: Model a closed set of exchange messages `AddOrder`, `CancelOrder`, `Trade` as a `std::variant` `using Msg = std::variant<AddOrder, CancelOrder, Trade>;`. Write the C++17 `overloaded` helper (with its deduction guide) and `char on_message(const Msg& m)` that uses `std::visit` to dispatch and return a one-char tag: `'A'` for AddOrder, `'C'` for CancelOrder, `'T'` for Trade. Note what happens if a fourth message type is added. The struct fields are fixed as shown in the starter.
hints: `template <class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; };`
Provide the deduction guide `overloaded(Ts...) -> overloaded<Ts...>;` for C++17.
coding.discussion: `overloaded` inherits `operator()` from each lambda (`using Ts::operator()...;` is a pack-expanded using-declaration), so the fused object is callable with any alternative and overload resolution picks the matching arm; the deduction guide lets you brace-construct it in C++17 (it's implicit in C++20). The `Msg` lives on the stack with no heap, no vtable, no RTTI, and `std::visit` is a jump table over the discriminant. Crucially, the dispatch is *exhaustive*: add a fourth alternative to `Msg` and the `std::visit` fails to compile until you handle it — exhaustiveness as a compile-time safety net. This is the HFT-preferred design over an inheritance hierarchy of heap-allocated message objects.

coding.prompt: Implement the strong-type pattern: a `template <class T, class Tag> struct Strong` with an `explicit` constructor and an `explicit` conversion operator back to `T`. Use it to define distinct `Price` and `Qty` types over `std::int64_t` and add `static_assert`s proving `sizeof(Price) == sizeof(std::int64_t)` and that it is trivially copyable. Mixing `Price` and `Qty` must be a compile error (the harness verifies the wrapper's behaviour at runtime).
hints: Empty tag structs make the instantiations distinct.
`explicit` on both the constructor and the conversion operator is essential.
coding.discussion: The `Tag` parameter makes `Strong<int64_t, PriceTag>` and `Strong<int64_t, QtyTag>` distinct types despite identical layout, so passing a `Qty` where a `Price` is expected is a build failure rather than a production incident. The `explicit` keywords on both the constructor and the `operator T()` are mandatory — drop either and you re-open the silent-conversion hole the plain alias had. The struct stays standard-layout and trivially copyable with the same size/alignment as the bare integer, so the safety is a compile-time fiction with zero runtime cost (verify with `static_assert` and the asm). Libraries like NamedType/type_safe add opt-in operator mixins so you don't hand-write the arithmetic.
